speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take this opportunity to comment on Bill C-110 and on the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). We have heard a great deal of debate and concern expressed by Members who have spoken about the way in which the Government of Canada seeks to assist Canadian businessmen in doing business overseas. I am convinced everyone here is concerned about the same thing, that Canada is competitive and able to take advantage of the opportunity which exists and realize our fair share, as much as we are able, of markets which exist for our products in other countries. Having said that, I think we need to re-examine for a moment what the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Regan) has been trying to do. He simply made a proposal to increase the number of Members on the Export Development Corporation Board from 12 to 15. The fundamental purpose of that change is to ensure a broad-range representation on that board and ensure it works as effectively and as thoroughly as possible, and to assist Canadian business people.
The amendment by the Hon. Member says that the Government should ensure that of those 15 members no more than 3 should come from the public sector. That in itself, Mr. Speaker, I think is a very serious affront not to this political Party or that political Party or whatever group happens to form, from a political point of view, the Government of the day, but an affront to a Public Service which has shown itself through the decades to be both highly competent, willing and able to work with the Government of the day in implementing Government policy. I say that not as a defence of a Liberal Government, I say that as a defence of and a respect for the civil service of this nation.
1 became somewhat concerned, Mr. Speaker, when I heard a few minutes ago the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), perhaps less diplomatically I would suggest than some of his colleagues, describe the Public Service of this country in a very unflattering way, in my estimation. The Public Service of Canada is based on the merit principle, and my mind reckons back to a newspaper article of May 11 when the Conservative leadership was still on and a candidate for that

September 13, 1983
Export Development Act
leadership, one Brian Mulroney, now the Hon. Member for Central Nova, the Leader of the Opposition, said at that time that when he becomes leader and when he becomes Prime Minister-a presumptious statement-

speakerposition: Deputy Opposition Whip; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: He has and he will.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
-there will be room for people of other political persuasions in this country to fill important roles in the Public Service but only after he has exhausted every single Tory in Canada. That, Mr. Speaker, is an amusing kind of statement which we tend to make in politics, but 1 hope it was only said in jest because if this proposed amendment is made in the spirit of ensuring that only three people whose abilities and service to this country are based on merit, not on partisan affiliation, can be allowed to serve on the board whose job is to assist Canadian business in doing business overseas, then I am a very disappointed man.
Let us look at some of the people from the public sector who should or could serve on that board, and who would be absolutely vital to ensuring that whatever private sector representatives are there, they are able to do as complete a job as possible. Who are some of those people? A representative from the Bank of Canada, perhaps the governor. That to me is a key Public Service appointment if this board is to be effective and not merely a bit if window dressing; a representative of the Minister of Trade's Department, of course; a representative from Industry, Trade and Commerce, of course; and a representative from CIDA, and this Department works with CIDA.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Pork-barrel.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
The Hon. Member's view of doing business overseas is politicized and is seen only through partisan eyes, Mr. Speaker.
If Canada is going to be successful in doing business, it is fundamental that a representative of the Department of Finance be on that board as well. These are key Government Departments which need to be represented. I want you to understand, Mr. Speaker, why I speak as 1 do today. If the Hon. Member for Mississauga South or any Member of this Party or any Party moved a motion to say that at least six members of the board had to be public servants, I would equally be opposed to having quotas. I think that what the Minister has provided is an increase from 12 to 15 members, and what he has said is that those 15 members should be the best people we can find, be they public or private, they should constitute as much as is possible the best mix of people to work together to enhance Canada's ability to do business overseas.

speakerposition: Deputy Opposition Whip; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: We will find someone to represent Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is the other key point, and I am glad the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) has raised that point. I hope that raising the number of people on the board from 12 to 15 would not make it an exclusive prerequisite of an appointment but, rather, that as much as possible, if not the Provinces then certainly the
regions of Canada, each of which has different and various resources, skills, products and expertise to offer, might perhaps be better represented on this kind of an advisory board.
In closing let me say again that I for one would be very concerned if a motion were moved that there must be six public servants, that there must be a quota, as I am now concerned to hear the Conservative Party saying there must be at least 12 to 15 appointments filled by the private sector. We in the House must get back to the notion that we can-
Socialism.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
No, not socialism but, rather, the mirror principle that we can best function when none of us becomes a blind, repetitive parrot for the extreme wing of our own extreme doctrinary position of our own particular philosophies. Is it not a rather embarrassing position to be standing up pounding one's fist across the way, saying that at least 12 of 15 key positions must be filled by those in private enterprise? It is a page from an extreme doctrine, a bible that is carried around.
I thank God 1 am not in a position to be a member of a Party which would take a position as the NDP might that at least 12 of 15 positions must be filled by those in the Public Service. I repeat that we must find the best mix and the best people based on the merit principle.
Once again I warn the Conservative Party and the Hon. Member for Central Nova (Mr. Mulroney) that the eyes of the people of Canada, now that he has entered the House, are very closely following his every utterance. The eyes and the ears of the people have seen his charismatic front and they want to know how deep it is. 1 would suggest that it is so shallow that I could walk across it with only a pair of slippers on and not even get my ankles wet. I warn him today that if I were made Prime Minister of this country, there would be room for merit only after every known partisan Tory has had an appointment. 1 shall warn him that the certainty and the cockiness with which he entered this Chamber will be deflated rapidly and much to his disappointment, and, of course, much to my delight.

Methinks the former speaker was preaching for a call. There is a vacancy in Newfoundland, I understand, in Canada's newest Province, and the great rhetoric that we have heard today, the great spirit of protection for the Public Service, will sit very well with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as he now shuffles a very small deck in Newfoundland as to who can be and who cannot be in the one Treasury Board seat that is left. You were very, very impressive, Brian. We all look forward to your progress in the days ahead.
Of course, being very serious, I would first of all like to say to the Minister that I have been very impressed with his energy and activities since he assumed that portfolio. It was my pleasure to be in the Philippines last weekend to meet with the Speaker and with the Minister and Vice Minister of Energy there and to hear their complimentary words about the
September 13, 1983

Minister's recent visit there with a significant number of very substantial business personalities from this country. On that trip they did business, and that is what his job is all about. Really, that is what the CDC is all about. It is a vehicle that is geared to assist our people in big business, in medium-sized business and in small business to move our products to the markets of the world. For, after all, we are traders. In many ways we are free traders. We are determined as exporters, as a basic exporting nation, to try to get our goods to the four corners of the earth. That is the case, and the EDC is a very significant vehicle because there is all kinds of competition out there by other nations against our goods. I am sure that the Minister realizes that more and more every day. Certainly, the more one visits the Pacific, the more one realizes just how difficult it is for our business community to compete against the emerging nations. It does not just involve Japan in the Pacific anymore; it involves the Republic of Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore. It is also starting to involve Indonesia and the Philippines. We must be there every day. I believe that the Minister, from his many experiences with the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, as Premier of the Province of Nova Scotia and in his present position, has a grasp of what is needed. However, I suggest that what is needed is not a bunch of civil servants, on this particular board.
One of the really sad things that I see about this nation that is not in evidence in many other nations is that we do not use all of the talent that we have available for as long as it is available. We have a system where everyone must sort of put one foot in the grave and the other on a banana peel once he becomes 65 years of age. There is a wealth of experience existing in Canada found in chairmen of boards and banks and in the small, medium and large industries in our country that is not being utilized.
The Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) pointed out a very significant example of what happened in Alberta with only two Government Members on a very significant board. I say to the Minister, let us go out there. I do not really believe that we can go to the sectors and ask businessmen to go on boards when there is any possibility of a conflict of interest or an unjust advantage to others in the same industries. However, I think that there are chairmen and presidents from Bell Canada and other corporations. One of the companies that the Minister and I both know very well is Northern Telecom. I happen to have the good fortune to have a Northern Telecom plant in my constituency. The Minister happened to be the Premier of Nova Scotia at the time that that plant was established. We both know what the then Chairman, Mr. Scribner, did for Canada. We know what Walter Light is doing for Canada now and Ben Benato. We know what others, especially in that sector of industry, know about the international marketing of products. As the Japanese often say, "Marketing is everything". Through vehicles like the EDC, we must assist those companies to get in there and meet the very heavy competition in the international world; for instance, Northern Teledon, without the same
Export Development Act
breadth and depth of a company like Seaman's, going in and beating it five times out of six. We must have people sitting on the EDC to be able to process applications with the snap of a finger. We do not want weeks and weeks of delay, double checking and looking to see that every T is crossed, which is the art and the style of civil servants. We have to give the background and the confidence to those people out there when they are in Singapore, in Germany, in Norway, or wherever they are, of knowing that they are going to have a board of directors, indeed, EDC, that will be with them all the way and will help and not hinder them. 1 think we have the kind of Minister who realizes that. I think the amendment is a good amendment. I think that puts you, Sir, where people cannot accuse you of political patronage when you are looking for directives. I think it puts you in a position where you are forced to be non-partisan, because everyone will be watching you and saying, "Let us see if the Minister is going to some big Grit or if he is going to give the private sector an opportunity and appoint the first best person who is available who is not implicated or involved in any way at this moment in his life." I think then we will be satisfied. The Minister will be satisfied. But, far more important, the people who are selling for us, earning the tax dollars for us so we can pay our other bills will be very confident in the Minister, they will be very confident in the Government and they will produce new jobs for the people. That is the bottom line for all of us right now and that is my contribution to the debate, Mr. Speaker.

If the Minister and the Government wanted to make progress, why would it not accept six directors covering all the important departments from the government services? That would leave nine to come from outside government services. Perhaps one might indicate that of those nine not more than two would come from any one province. All the Provinces are interested in trade. This would ensure fair regional distribution. Representation would not be all from the finance sector on Bay Street in Toronto or all from the manufacturing sector in Toronto or all from some other area. But that is the type of compromise 1 am thinking of. If we are really serious in trying to make government work, this is a way to compromise and trade off a little bit, and I think through that process we sometimes get the best result. I would invite the Minister or his Parliamentary Secretary to go part way on this suggestion. Even at this stage, and perhaps with all-Party consent, we could agree to the Government's own amendment if it would go part way, as long as majority representation would be from the private sector. Otherwise we will have people paid by the taxpayer, public servants, controlling the public Crown Corporations, and it becomes a bit incestuous to have them controlling a publicly owned corporation because they have something at stake. It is too narrow a base. Therefore, I recommend that the Government consider a halfway measure between the position as drafted in the Bill and this amendment. I think that might be of some assistance.
I want to put one example on the record about why I feel it is important. I was very frustrated on one occasion with an industry in my own constituency and an industry that was based in Nova Scotia, namely, Pioneer Electric. Through Canadian Patents and Development Ltd. this company got rights to market ground detectors for hospital operating rooms. The device was invented by the National Research Council people. It was an extremely important device. Ten to 15 years ago people died on operating tables. Death was put down to heart fibrillations, but it was not heart fibrillations, it was electric shock. So much equipment was attached to people in the operating process. With a little electric leakage from each machine enough current was finally built up so that a person was electrocuted. What was developed at the National Research Council and what Pioneer Electric and Canadian Stackpole's Measurment Engineering division in Arnprior had the right to do was to market the device and pay royalties to CPDL. Unfortunately, after they paid a little over $100,000 in royalties, a firm set up in Clearwater, Florida copied the patents which CPDL had. These patents were registered in the United States. An investigation was started as to whether we should stop them. I have three legal opinions from American patent attorneys who said that Canadian Patents and Development Ltd. would be successful in their suit. But they were controlled by employees of the corporation and other members on the board who were public servants. Only a few were from the private sector. They did not have enough gumption to go ahead. If they had paid $60,000 they would have made another $100,000 in royalties from the successful sales. Instead, no prosecution took place. The other people in Clearwater ended up stealing our patent, going ahead and expanding further. They were subsequently bought out by a company called Square D. Square D is a big electrical contracting firm. Square D up to that point in time had been buying 60 per cent of the manufactured product from Canadian Stackpole and Pioneer Engineering. We lost the market. Since this technique was developed, every hospital operating room in North America and around the world had to have one of these devices. It was a tremendous market and we blew it because we were too timid.
If we had had a few more aggressive businessmen on the board, they might have taken that further step and assured the manufacturing rights for Canadians, not letting them slip away as in this case.
I suggest a compromise be considered. The Parliamentary Secretary said we do not want too narrow a base. If we have too large a majority from the public sector, it would be too narrow a base. But perhaps we could have a group from the public sector covering those six important departmental areas and the other nine directors spread fairly well across Canada, maybe two from Quebec, two from Ontario, two from Nova Scotia, one in Saskatchewan or one from Ontario, but not more than two from any one province. This is my suggestion. I am not bound to it; I am just making a suggestion. If the Government wants three for any one province, they can have three. I wanted to make the point that it should be spread out across Canada to ensure that we do not have too small a base from which to work. I think the Government should consider it. Perhaps we could get on to the next amendment; hopefully the Government is willing to make some movement.

Mr. Speaker,
I am very pleased to rise to lend a few observations to this very important debate on our approach as Canadians to the promotion of export trade and to the established and recognized role of the Export Development Corporation in achieving those goals. In particular I rise to speak to Motion No. 1, sponsored by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), which takes a rather different approach to the structuring of the board of directors of the EDC than that put forward in the present legislation. The proposal of my colleague would ensure a dominant private sector emphasis on the board of directors. Of course we assume that these people would be well qualified in their disciplines, would represent an appropriate cross-section of the business and corporate community and would ensure that the EDC fulfil the objectives we all wish as Canadians. This is a very important agency of Government which, throughout the past decade or more of its existence, has made a number of errors, many of which have cost Canadian taxpayers dearly.
I will get into specific examples of those errors in a moment, but 1 think it is important to ask ourselves what is the role of the Export Development Corporation. Should it be a promoter of Canadian trade in other parts of the world for the benefit of Canadians? Should it be an extension of our foreign aid
September 13, 1983

initiatives, perhaps operating on the same principle as the Canadian International Development Agency to assist the emergence and development of less privileged nations around the world? It is important for us as Canadians, particularly in these difficult economic times, to realize that our first obligation is to get our own economic house in order and put Canadians back to work. As our level of prosperity improves and as Canada is restored once again to the point where we can make genuine technological, scientific and social contribution to the needs of those less fortunate than ourselves, perhaps we can put an increased emphasis upon foreign aid.
The purpose of the EDC at this point in time should be to enhance and increase the opportunity for Canadian businesses to penetrate more aggressively markets around the world and thereby overcome the serious unemployment crisis in Canada. If that is to be our goal, we must ask ourselves whether the EDC has been effective and honest with its masters, the Parliament and the Government of Canada, in submitting to the House cost analyses so that Canadians know on an annualized basis whether there is a net return for the moneys expended by way of loan guarantees and other forms of assistance to Canadian corporations. 1 mean a net return; in other words, for every dollar spent by Canadian taxpayers they should know whether there has been a multiplier effect operating in that we received more than a dollar back to be used toward the needs of Canada and toward a solution to our serious unemployment problem. If we want to make the EDC an instrument of foreign aid, that is fine, but let us face up to the truth and tell Canadians that that is what it is.
I will turn to the question of the amendment and whether the board of the EDC and its president and chief executive officer, Mr. Cloutier, has been doing an effective job over the years in ensuring that this goal is achieved. Personally I find it repugnant to watch, as we did in recent years-not in the last year or so-colossal advertising campaigns by the Export Development Corporation geared to Canadian consumers. 1 never understood why there were full-page ads in national and local newspapers and television advertisements promoting the aims and objectives of the EDC. Those initiatives were an absolute waste of taxpayers' money because they were directed at the wrong market. What difference does it make if the Canadian television viewer or newspaper reader is sold on how great is the EDC? Its customers are the corporations of Canada. They should be the benefactors, and ultimately the workers of Canada. If one examined the philosophy behind those advertising campaigns, one would realize that they were nothing more than a glorified back-slapping exercise on the part of the Liberal Government in its attempt to brainwash Canadians into believing that everything it does is for the good of every last one of us. As with many of the travesties to which the Government has exposed Canadians in the name of advertising, it was absolutely unnecessary. It is an example of the kind of decision private sector members of the board would never have permitted. It was an absolute waste of taxpayers' money which did very little to achieve the goals of the EDC.

For a moment I would like to look at what has happened in the Canadian mineral industry over the past 20 years to 25 years and to what extent the EDC has contributed to the situation. In 1950, nickel world-wide was produced by three countries-Canada, the U.S.S.R. and Australia. The Sudbury basin in Ontario produced sulphide ores, and laterite ores were produced in New Caledonia, Australia. As of last year the inventory of nickel producers world-wide rose to some 25 different nations producing and refining nickel. Many of these refineries were subsidized by government largesse, much of it extended by this nation to promote the development of mining activities in other parts of the world. If we believe that the EDC should be an instrument of foreign aid, then that is a very admirable gesture. But we have increased the production capacity of nickel to the point where we are on the verge of seeing the Canadian nickel industry collapse. The same is true in the case of copper, coal and many other mineral industries where we used the instruments of CIDA and EDC to help, aid, abet and build ports and new projects around the world. I am not saying that we should not do this. I am saying that we should analyse whether there is a net benefit or a net cost to Canada inherent in such initiatives.
I would like to refer to a particular example concerning a coal mining project in Indonesia about which the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) crowed quite loudly on May 4 of this year. Canada was signing an agreement through the EDC to finance the development of a major new coal mine in Indonesia. In fact, the Minister was present in Jakarta for the signing of the contract under which Canadian companies would receive certain spin-off benefits in relation to the development of the coal mining project in southern Sumatra, Indonesia. The fact of the matter is that we are aiding and abetting the creation of an additional nine million tonnes of coal production capacity in another country. That country requires in return that it be given access to an equivalent dollar value of business in Canada. In other words, one of the terms of the deal under which we guaranteed low interest financing for the opening of that new coal mine in Indonesia is that it does a reciprocal amount of business in Canada. There is no net gain for Canada in such an initiative. This new mine will exceed the production capacity of one of the largest mines in British Columbia of which there are only three or four. I will be taking my seat in a moment, but let me first indicate that we will in fact experience a net loss. We will lose many jobs as a result of the additional competition which this mine will pose.
In conclusion I would suggest that if the board of directors of the Export Development Corporation included a healthy dose of representation from the private sector, we would take a much more quantitative approach to determining whether these kinds of decisions are wise, because in that case Canada would emerge as a net loser.

Mr. Speaker, the presentation of this Bill is an expression of interest in international trade and the vehicle by which it could be accomplished.

September 13, 1983
Export Development Act
However, the Bill is only an expression of mechanics, not an expression of policy as it has been exercised by the Government. I would like to discuss that policy as it relates to this Bill and to international trade in general. I hope that the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) will take the time to listen. I fully appreciate his total duties and responsibilities, but I would like to get this message to him because Atlantic Canada is deeply concerned about a situation which is now arising in our international trade with the United States.
As a result of representations made by the State of Maine, the United States Department of Trade has undertaken hearings and has made recommendations on the basis of information gathered at those hearings to the effect that there should be a 17.9 per cent duty-type impost levied on white potatoes shipped to the United States from eastern Canada, as far west as the Great Lakes.
What is the impact of this ruling? It is a virtual embargo because of the level of the assessment which has been made. It is a virtual embargo upon the exportation of potatoes from Canda into the United States. This breaks the spirit of trade relations which have existed between Canada and the United States.
1 want to make clear that I have tried to get information on the meetings to be held in the United States to give further and final consideration to the impost which has been imposed upon us. To this point, I have not been able to find anybody who had at their fingertips information on a succession of meetings which will consider the subject matter. I have not been able to find anybody who can tell me whether we can or cannot make representations on behalf of Canada at these hearings. That is a situation which is intolerable. It defines a policy which is unacceptable to Canadian agriculture which must have export trade if it is to survive.
I want to point out something else. If we are to survive economically, we must have a better balance of trade in the horticulture industry. We have reached the point where, with the United States alone, we have approximately $700 million annual deficit in trade of horticultural products.
There is a traditional trading pattern in commodities which are traded throughout the world. There is a world price or continental price and commodities are traded on the basis of that price. In Canada only when vital emergencies arise do we have the authority to impose any constraint of trade upon any of our GATT partners, only when the Department has declared a real emergency in a particular commodity.
Let me cite an example. The British Columbia potato industry is very detrimentally affected by the importation of potatoes from the State of Washington. Our Government has said that it is not possible to establish that dumping operations are taking place as these potatoes come from the State of Washington to the Province of British Columbia. In spite of this, we are found guilty of dumping and damage in the United States, according to the recent ruling of the Department of Trade and Commerce in that area.
More hearing are to be held. I believe the final hearing of the international trade commission of the United States is to be held on October 30. If the horticultural industry of Canada does not have the total support of information and legal advice from the Government of Canada, with all the statistics to back it up, we will be faced with a further unfavourable ruling. This will occur if we cannot present our case as the situation exists at the moment.
I cannot get from the officials responsible for this operation the scheduling or subject matter of these meetings. I am very disappointed. It makes me think that this Bill may be just more window dressing. Is that what it is, or will it play to a particular segment of Canadian international trade and ignore the agricultural sphere of Canada?
The agricultural sphere has traditionally been put in a second rate position in the trading pattern of this nation. We have traded off this item in return for some import regulation, export regulation, or something else. The Government has said consistently and persistently that it will give the United States better access to Canada with the foods it produces in return for which we hope to get a better opportunity to export some manufactured goods. This has continued to the point where we cannot stand embargoes such as the one presently being imposed upon us by the United States. It is not an embargo by name, but it is virtually an embargo.
In an effort to defend ourselves against this action, we do not know what formula has been used to arrive at the figure known as a constructive value in the United States. We know that shippers in Canada have been accused of dumping. Internationally, dumping is accepted as the shipping of a product abroad at a lesser price than it would be shipped to a domestic customer. The shipping industry in Canada would have to be nuts to do any dumping. Why sell abroad at greater commercial risk at a price lower than you would sell in Canada?
1 have been directly involved with that industry almost since birth. Any dealer in the potato industry who ships potatoes from Canada to the United States does so because the market is better there; he will get more money for his product than he could get in Canada. Therefore, under the literal international interpretation of the term "dumping" we are not guilty of it in any way, shape or form. I have confidence that our dealers have economic sanity even in restricted markets.
I wish to say to the Minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that ever since the transportation capability has existed allowing us to exchange food products with our neighbours to the south, we have had what is known as a continental market and a continental price. If a commodity produced in Canada is marketed, it is under the influence of the continental price, not a Canadian price per se. If the ruling handed down by the United States Trade Department is imposed, it will reverse the accepted trading patterns between these two nations which has existed since the earlier trade in foods, particularly horticultural products.
We have been accused of dumping. However, in the assessment of dumping, 1 would ask whether the sale was made today, six months ago, two months ago and whether the
September 13, 1983

market was at the same level at which it is today. Did the investigators take into consideration the possibility of a future sale? Did they understand the difference between an f.o.b. sale and a delivered sale? Is that the way they arrived at the fact that M. Rose and Sons is accused of dumping to the extent of 20 some percentage points? If it was in fact guilty-Mr. Speaker, 1 see that my time is running out. I wonder if I could have unanimous consent to make a very few brief remarks to conclude?

speechtext: Is there consent for the Hon. Member to extend his remarks?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There appears to be.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank Members of the House.
If M. Rose and Sons was in fact guilty of conducting most of its trade during the last year with the United States and if in fact it sold at a price that was 22 per cent or 23 per cent less than what the Canadian market could afford, M. Rose and Sons would not be in business today. It is as simple as that. The very fact that M. Rose and Sons is still in business contradicts the accused margin of dumping.
Is the Marshall Company in Ontario guilty of dumping by 41 per cent? If it had in fact dumped into the United States at 41 per cent less than the Canadian market could have afforded, its officers are certainly candidates for an insane asylum and they must today be bankrupt by virtue of their idiotic trade policies.
The conclusions which have been reached contradict all logic, Mr. Speaker, and I appeal to the Minister of State for International Trade to ensure that this matter have the highest possible profile and support for the representations to be made.
I am being parochial when I mention potatoes because potatoes are the bread and butter of my community, but I am not being parochial when I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that there are further representations ready to be made by further commodity producers in the United States that might in fact have the same capability of getting protection from their Government which will interfere with the exports of Canadian agricultural products across the board. If the decision is unfavourable to Canada with respect to potatoes, then one can expect equally unfavourable decisions with respect to other food products which may be shipped to them.
1 appeal to the Government and to the Minister that we do now activate every force that the Government has at its disposal to try to use the goodwill which we have established in so many ways in the United States to establish the innocence of the commodity trade as it relates to potatoes and as it will later relate to other commodities and to accept the traditional fact that commodities are marketed world-wide, not in relation to cost in any given year nor in relation to storage costs or shipping costs or any other costs but are internationally mar-
Export Development Act
keted between Canada and the United States and the world on the basis of the price that prevails on the date the sale is made. If we begin to interfere with that, Mr. Speaker, then I say to you that Canada and the United States will be in positions of extreme difficulty with respect to trading on a very broad basis. This is not acceptable.
We in Canada from coast to coast must ask that the Government make the strongest possible representations on this matter to the authorities of the United States who I believe want our good will and are probably not aware of the ultimate consequence of a single item. When looking back 13 years, we find that it is an item of which we have imported more from the United States in volume than from any other nation. We have imported more from them in 10 out of the 13 years. We have spent more in the United States on potatoes than they have spent in Canada in 11 out of the 13 years. Even with potatoes, the balance of trade is, on average, well in their favour. I ask that these representations be made and that the matter be taken seriously by the Cabinet.

Mr. Speaker, although I have listened to this debate all day, I did not intend to speak to this Bill until the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin), the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister responsible for this Bill, spoke, and he began speaking using rising decibels-
No, he is not my Parliamentary Secretary.

Someone said that he was the Parliamentary Secretary and I took his word for it. He began speaking to this Bill using rising decibels. 1 suppose that being from Newfoundland, he wanted to make sure or at least hope that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), from the bowels of the PMO, would hear that there was yet another Member from Newfoundland who might qualify for a Cabinet post now that two of them have been discarded in the last month.
The Hon. Member was concerned about the proposal that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), presented to the Minister regarding the membership of the board of directors for the Export Development Corporation. The Government proposal ensures that the majority of those members are drawn from Government offices, the bureaucracy. My colleague proposes that a majority of them be drawn from the private sector. My friend from Newfoundland wonders what is wrong with having most of them come from the Government offices. There is nothing morally wrong with that. However, the fact is that that usually does not work very well. It is not that it has been without success, but the batting average is probably not very good.
The reason that the success rate is not very good is that there is a difference between the mind-set of those members on a board of directors who come from Government offices and that of those who come from the private sector. They have different mind sets, different philosophies, different reasons for being there and, perhaps, different ideologies. Mainly, they have different reasons for being there.

September 13, 1983
Export Development Act
A Government official's reason for being on a board of directors is very simple and very honourable, and it is to protect the taxpayers' money. He wants to make sure that the investments are secure, that they will be above reproach, that he will not fall under any kind of criticism and that the Government will fall under a minimum amount of criticism as a result of these investments.
Goodness knows 1 wish some of these people would have had some say in the investment in the Maislin Corporation and in a few other large grants that the Government has made outside of the parameters of these lending agencies. Obviously the lending agencies had nothing to do with those kinds of grants.
The reason the Government official is there is to make sure that the investment is secure, and if it is secure, to avoid political criticism and mistakes as much as possible, and that is a good reason for his being there. However, that is not the function of that organization. That is not why that organization exists.
Obviously the investments ought to be as secure as possible, but there are other ingredients to an investment corporation and one other ingredient is that there ought to be some risk. Those two principles do not mix very well when there are two opposing kinds of people on the board.
Let me use as an illustration the national banks that are now in many cases riding herd on some of the companies that are in trouble across the land as a result of the recession. Here is company "X" with, let us say, $2 million worth of capital investment. It is now just at the point of having as much debt as equity. The banks get nervous and the bank bureaucracies are no different from Government bureaucracies. They get twitchy. What do they do? Do they come and say, "Let us get some creative people in this organization to help you out so that you will have a better cash flow"? No, they send out a bank auditor who knows nothing about the business and whose one purpose is to make sure that the bank's investment is secure and not to make sure that the company will succeed. They want to retrieve as much as possible of the bank's investment.
1 submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that that kind of mentality is parallel to or at least similar to the kind of mind-set that the Government official has when he sits on a board of investment such as this. The board member from the private sector, however, has an entirely different approach to business. Obviously he wants his investment to be secure-no one is in business to lose money-but he also has a willingness to take a creative risk. He does not mind risking in order to succeed, if necessary.
On a national scale, one of the problems in this country is that we do not risk easily enough. That is why we have billions of dollars of foreign investment in the country. Per capita, Canadians have more money in the bank than any other country in the world. Canadians do not want to take risks and prefer the safe route. The Export Development Corporation
cannot succeed if it has the mindset of a Government bureaucracy that is afraid to take a risk.
There is another reason why it is not good to have a majority of Government officials on the board of directors. It was indicated in a different way by the Hon. Member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon). He pointed out that not too long ago the Export Development Corporation funded a coal mining venture in Sumatra for which Canada would provide the equipment. In the process, Sumatra will become competitive with the coal mines of British Columbia. I suspect that if a majority of the board of directors of the Export Development Corporation had had the marketplace in mind rather than the immediate sale of equipment, they would not have funded a mining operation that would cut out domestic interests. This is an investment on an international scale that in the long run will hurt the domestic market.
I submit that if there were more members from the private sector on the board of directors of the corporation and they were sensitive to domestic trade, an investment would not have been made that would cut off trade within Canada.
For these reasons the amendment submitted by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South is a good one. 1 would ask Members of the Government to be open-minded about the whole proposition. There was a day when the Party opposite had the marketplace and free enterprise as its hallmark. It has shifted its focus and is now looking at security by way of Government departments and Government officials.
I support this amendment, Mr. Speaker, because it would introduce some creativity into the investment market for the Export Development Corporation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald Regan (Minister of State (International Trade)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), first of all I want to thank all Hon. Members who have spoken on it today. There have been some excellent interventions and only a few things have been expressed with which I can seriously disagree.
I believe that the interest exhibited in the importance of the export industry is heartening and appropriate in relation to the role exports play in the creation of jobs in Canada. I am sure you are cognizant of the fact, Mr. Speaker, that, more than any other advanced industrialized country, Canada depends on the sale of goods and services in overseas markets for the standard of living we enjoy. It would not be available to us if over two million Canadians were not employed as a consequence of exports. I believe we can do even better than we have to date to develop export markets for our goods and services.
The intention of the amendment is the provide the Export Development Corporation-which is one of a number of ways in which the Government assists exporters in this country-to do a better job than it has been able to until now.
Before I enter into a discussion of what has been said and attempt to react to some of the comments made, I want to take advantage of this opportunity to congratulate the Hon.
September 13, 1983

Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight), who participated in the debate, upon his nomination as shadow Cabinet critic for international trade. During his time in Parliament he has been an outstanding Member and I know he will bring great ability to the job. 1 look forward to his comments and assistance in this particular task.
I also want to congratulate his associate critic, the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker), who also spoke in the debate. He also has made a mark as an able Member in his time in the House. 1 am gratified that people who are constructive and able have received these assignments for what I consider to be a very important portfolio.
During the time that the Bill was in committee it received very careful consideration and lengthy examination. A number of other Hon. Members opposite have shown interest in the subject in committee and in the House. I particularly commend the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blen-karn) who has shown a very keen interest in the Bill and in bringing forward suggestions for ways in which it could be improved, according to his judgment. 1 want to emphasize that because, even though 1 am unable to accept the particular amendment that he has proposed, I agree and applaud the principle of greater private sector participation in the Export Development Corporation. I propose to follow that principle in my dealings with the board.
1 cannot agree, however, with the principle of codification or, if you like, a statutory quota for how the board of directors of a Crown corporation should be made up. 1 do not believe we should tie the hands of future Governments with reference to how appointments are to be made. Appointments should be made from the private or public sector according to the talent that is available at a particular time and according to the ability of the people available. That is a principle that has been followed traditionally in all Crown corporations, I believe.
I have always thought that if we are to have Crown corporations-and certainly the EDC is one that is necessary for reasons that are plain-we should set them up so that they can operate with the flexibility of a private company and with as few strings as possible. That is the way to achieve the healthy atmosphere of private enterprise in a Government-owned company.
1 want to emphasize that while the Export Development Corporation is vital for its work in financing our exports, no one should be under the illusion that it is the only organization that is financing exports. It finances only a very small portion of total Canadian exports. The vast portion of this financing is done by the private banking system, as it should be. We have the situation, however, that the banks are often unwilling or unable, for good reason, to do the long-term financing that may be required to enable us to achieve the major overseas sales which bring a great number of jobs to Canada and benefits to our companies. It is in that area primarily that EDC has the greatest validity, and I believe that most Hon. Members of the House recognize its importance in that regard.
Export Development Act
I would like to say, in response to the concerns of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South, which have been reflected by other Hon. Members who have spoken on this matter, that I agree with the principle that the majority of directors of EDC should come from the private sector. I feel it is a good idea, and as long as I am minister I can assure him that I will do all I can to ensure that that will be the case, that the majority will be appointed from the private sector.
I believe that in enlarging the board to 15, we are not only making it possible for us to be in the position of ensuring a majority from the private sector, but also of ensuring the regional representation of which some Hon. Members have spoken as well. That, I believe, is also important. What I do want to say, however, is that the public sector directors who participate on the board, in my opinion, do a very valuable job, and I feel their work is important. There seems to have been some misconception by one or two Hon. Members who thought these directors were people who came from the EDC itself. That, of course, is not the case. It is not a question of employees running their own organization. It is, rather, the importance which has been recognized by successive Governments of having the key financial agencies of Government represented by able people on the Export Development Corporation, if it is going to have the full co-operation of those branches of Government and be best able to serve the exporters of our country.

However, we have gone beyond that and said that when there is an important opportunity which is of net benefit to the Canadian public, where it is shown to us that a competitor is breaking the consensus or offering a concessional rate, we should examine whether it is in the interests of Canada to match that. And in examining whether it is in Canada's interests, one would have to determine whether the jobs which would be created were a better price than the other sort of job creation on which we spend money through various Government departments, and whether the net benefit to Canada makes it worth-while. subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS-CAPITALIZATION OF CORPORATIONS. (B) USE OF LETTERS OF COMFORT
CROWN CORPORATIONS-CAPITALIZATION OF CORPORATIONS. (B) USE OF LETTERS OF COMFORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I missed my opportunity to speak on the motion on Bill C-110 but I have my opportunity now to talk about a very similar subject, that of Crown corporations and the Government's practice of providing letters of comfort.
For myself and many of my colleagues this all came to light this spring when we had the unfortunate experience of witnessing one of the greatest financial travesties in this country, namely the collapse of Canadair and de Havilland. In my riding, Mr. Speaker, the people do not understand how much $2 billion is, let alone $500 million. In their minds that would be enough money to build industry to create jobs not only for every person in my riding but possibly for two or three surrounding ridings.
On June 22, 1983, I asked the Minister whether it was common practice to operate Crown corporations by letters of comfort. At that time I got no answer. Upon checking through the two Crown corporations I referred to, I found this had been carried on over an extended period of time. This, Mr. Speaker, to the citizens of this country is as immoral as printing money without coming before this House for approval. If you are going to have borrowing bills, then this method of providing money should be dealt with in the same way.
Letters of comfort, Mr. Speaker, are guarantees from the federal Government to Canadian and international banks. This is not only taking capital out of the country, it is also taking the interest on that capital out of the country. It increases the debt we owe to the rest of the world as well as to Canadians, and I feel this practice should be stopped.
In the Bill we have just been discussing, which we object to, Mr. Speaker, there is no accountability to the House of Commons. The same situation pertains to these letters of comfort. On June 22, I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) to table in this House the number of Crown corporations financed by letters of comfort. I would like to extend that. I not only want to know the number, I would like to know the names and I would also like to know the individual amounts. The reason I cut the question short is that Madam Speaker is so in tune with what is happening she cuts us off rather quickly and we have to be very concise with our questions, and sometimes we do not the entire question in.
To me, Mr. Speaker, receiving a letter of comfort is the same thing as taking money out of the back door of the bank. In that way no one seems to know about it. There is another method that perhaps the Government could use instead of letters of comfort, that is through computer mystique, comput-

September 13, 1983
Adjournment Debate
er disappearance. Perhaps that is how the Government should be getting the money to run these Crown corporations. I do not know, Mr. Speaker, but it is a thought. Now that we have nailed them down on this one, they will find a new method. But any time, Mr. Speaker, that the Government goes into the taxpayers' pockets and removes $1.4 billion, in the case of Canadair, it must be accountable to the House of Commons.
It would be marvellous for Canadian corporations and small businesses to be able to operate under letters of comfort, Mr. Speaker. Can one imagine what would happen if a proliferation of letters of comfort were allowed? Supposing a small businessman having trouble went to his Member of Parliament and said, "I require a letter of comfort because my company is almost in bankruptcy." Where would it stop?
Let us take another example. In every Department of Government, there are hidden corporations, some of which we have not even been able to locate. There is a budget put down in the Estimates by which Departments are supposed to live. Those corporations could funnel more cash into that Department through the back door, thus increasing budgets over and above the original Estimates.
I do not know how many other games are being played and perpetuated on the Canadian public. However, I do not believe this is the only one. Furthermore, from June 22 to this day, I do not have a record of what this money is, what has been going out, how much and to whom.
Let us take another example of a letter of comfort, and truly a letter of comfort as it is used, involving $34 million more for Maislin Transport. That is another letter of comfort, another name for a guarantee. That one went down the tube.
I must really ask another question. How many other guarantees are out to the private sector that have never come before this House because they are too small in amount to be considered? I think the Auditor General is aware of this situation. He is watching for it. However, it is something he cannot track down because it is done outside of his terms of reference. He must check the audits of the Department. He does not even have the right to audit Crown corporations until the Opposition stands in the House and demands that it be done.
I would therefore like to see the entire Government format changed, the financial responsibility changed, and letters of comfort discontinued. In order to prove this point, I would today like to see the list I requested on June 22 with the updated information I requested.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Lang (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS-CAPITALIZATION OF CORPORATIONS. (B) USE OF LETTERS OF COMFORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue of letters of comfort has been discussed at some length over the past year, especially at the Standing Senate Committee on National Finance. Consequently, much of what I am about to say has already been reported to that Committee.
As Members are aware, it is the Government's current policy to issue letters of comfort only in those instances where
Parliamentary authority for a guarantee does not yet exist but where it is the Government's intention to seek such authority. Approval to issue a letter of comfort is given by Governor in Council upon the recommendation of the Treasury Board and subject to the approval of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) of the terms and conditions of the borrowing in question.
Letters of comfort have been used in the past to assist both Canadair and de Havilland to borrow funds until such time as guarantees could be issued, de Havilland, for example, borrowed $70 million on the basis of a letter of comfort issued on December 24, 1976 by the then Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, for the production of the Dash-7 aircraft. The letter of comfort, with an expiry date of December 31, 1980, was extended to September, 1981, at which time it was no longer required. Appropriation Act No. 4, 1980-81 authorized the guarantee of loans to de Havilland to a limit of $450 million and no further letters of comfort have been issued for de Havilland.
Canadair has used letters of comfort since its purchase by the Crown in 1976 when an operating line of credit was issued to Canadair covered by a letter of comfort issued by the then Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The Challenger program was approved by the government in October, 1976, and financial arrangements were made for a further line of credit supported by a loan guarantee authorized by Appropriation Acts No. 5, 1976-77 and No. 3, 1977-78.
In June, 1978, refinancing of the guaranteed loan and the Challenger special operating line of credit was enabled through the issue of a letter of comfort.
By March, 1979, an additional loan was secured by a letter of comfort and an increase in cash requirements by September, 1979, resulted in a loan guarantee authorized by Appropriation Act No. 1, 1980-81.
By April, 1981, the company identified further cash requirements and Treasury Board recommended an additional letter of comfort to be issued and replaced upon Parliamentary approval of further loan guarantees. In September, 1981, Treasury Board again recommended further interim letters of comfort to be replaced upon Parliamentary approval of loan guarantees. This authority was obtained in Appropriation Act No. 4, 1981-82, with the result that the interim letters of comfort will either be replaced by the guarantees or will be allowed to expire.
Currently, there are two outstanding letters of comfort for Canadair supporting two loans totalling $130 million (U.S.). The total value of loans, either guaranteed or supported by letters of comfort, are within the Parliamentary authorized $1.35 billion guarantee ceiling.
There is one other letter of comfort outstanding, bringing the total to three at this time. This letter of comfort was issued to support a $150 million loan in Canadian funds of Ridley Terminals Limited, a company 90 per cent owned by National Harbours Board. The letter of comfort was issued on September 14, 1982, and is currently in the process of being replaced.
September 13, 1983

Mr. Speaker, on June 15 last, I had occasion to ask a question of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr Bussieres), who reports to the House for the Minister of State for Social Development, with respect to Canadair Limited and certain moneys that had been transferred on that date to Canadair in the amount of $240 million.
Your Honour will recall that in December of 1982 the House advanced $200 million to Canadair. In June of this year we advanced $240 million. Of course, following the question placed on June 15, there were a number of meetings with the Public Accounts Committee where Canadair attempted to explain itself through the new owner of that company or the purported owner of that company or the imputed owner of that company, an organization calling itself the Canada Development Investment Corporation, a corporation that has yet to receive any Parliamentary authority, but one authored and operated by one Joel Bell of National Energy Board fame.
All of the evidence brought to the Public Accounts Committee indicated that we had only given a short term transfusion to Canadair in June. We gave it $240 million then. subtopic: ENERGY-SALES OF WESTERN COAL IN CENTRAL CANADA. (B) REQUEST FOR COST STUDY OF COAL USE
ENERGY-SALES OF WESTERN COAL IN CENTRAL CANADA. (B) REQUEST FOR COST STUDY OF COAL USE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been almost three months since I raised a question in the House concerning the use of western Canadian coal to supply eastern Canadian markets. On June 16 I pointed out to the House, and specifically to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), that Canada imports approximately 16 million tonnes of coal every year from the United States. We import all that coal despite the fact that we are one of the world's great coal producers. We pay an enormous price for
that imported coal. Each year a billion dollars flows out of the country to pay for that imported coal. Along with that billion dollars we lose approximately 30,000 jobs in Canada.
In return for that enormous loss of jobs, what do we get? We get massive pollution problems because imported American coal has eight times the sulphur content of Canadian coal. This extra sulphur goes directly into acid rain. In spite of these enormous costs and consequences, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources refused even to give the question a serious answer. Instead we were treated to the stupid response that Canada's rail facilities could not handle both coal and wheat at the same time, something he said changing the Crow rate would improve.
If the Minister knew his geography, he would know that the main problems of the rail transportation system are in western Canada. In southeastern British Columbia and in Alberta one has to travel large distances before one hits the main traffic of the railway system. This would not affect rail transportation in any way whatsoever.
1 gave the Minister notice of the question. If he had tried to find out something about it, he would have discovered that the change in the Crow rate would have absolutely nothing to do with shipping coal east on southern railway lines. He might even have found out that the Japanese, one of our major customers, have demanded that their Canadian suppliers absorb cuts in both the sales of coal and its price. I would have thought the possibility of 30,000 new jobs in Canada and the saving of $1 billion flowing out of this country would have been worth at least that much work on the part of the Minister. Perhaps, because most of these jobs would be created in western Canada, the Minister, like his colleagues, simply does not care.
On behalf of all Canadians, particularly the unemployed miners in western Canada, I again ask whether the Minister will have his Department carry out an extensive study to determine the feasibility of using western coal to supply eastern Canadian markets as a replacement for imported American coal? Will the Minister ensure that such a study includes the very real costs of increased acid rain as a result of using imported American coal?

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-SALES OF WESTERN COAL IN CENTRAL CANADA. (B) REQUEST FOR COST STUDY OF COAL USE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened to the Hon. Member I want to assure him that I share his concern that quantities of western coal are not being utilized in central Canada. I point out to him that there is a large body of coal in eastern Canada, namely the Maritimes, which would like to find its way to market in central Canada as well.
Unfortunately the Hon. Member refuses, intentionally or otherwise, to accept some of the arguments which are economic in substance. Earlier today we heard from the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan), who at one point in his career was the Premier of Nova Scotia. On numerous
September 13, 1983

occasions he tried diligently to attempt to get eastern coal into the markets of central Canada. Unfortunately, he was not successful, primarily because of the economics of shipping the coal from eastern to central Canada. Likewise, the argument holds for shipping coal from western Canada to central Canada.
Due to the size and geography of this country, Canada has long been a coal trader. During 1982, Canada exported 16 million tonnes of coal valued at $1.2 billion and imported 15.7 million tonnes at approximately $1.2 billion. While Canada is currently a net coal exporter both in terms of volume and value of coal, exports have been forecasted to grow in the future and imports are expected to drop.
1 wish to assure the Hon. Member that I will take under advisement his suggestion, and pursue it with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien). However, I do not want the opportunity to go by without saying that we have already looked at the various possibilities. The Hon. Member
Adjournment Debate
must remember that Ontario Hydro is not owned or operated by the Government of Canada, but by the Province of Ontario. It is they in their wisdom who will determine whether they will purchase coal from western Canada, in his instance, or in my instance, from eastern Canada.
The Hon. Member makes a valid point that the Government should consider re-examining this. I assure him I will raise this point with the Minister. If anything can be done, 1 am sure this government will attempt to do it in order to assist not only the people of western Canada but of eastern Canada. As he knows, it would provide much in terms of job creation at this time in our economy.
